CVE-2026-104259.title: ModSecurity: removeComments Transformation Fails to Strip Adjacent Comments, Enabling WAF Rule Bypass
CVE-2026-104259.description: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx. Prior to 2.9.15 and 3.0.17, msre_fn_removeComments_execute in apache2/re_tfns.c and inplace() in src/actions/transformations/remove_comments.cc implement t:removeComments by copying the character immediately after a comment terminator without re-evaluating it. Adjacent comments can therefore leave a later comment in the transformed value, allowing inline-comment obfuscation to bypass rules that depend on comment stripping. When a comment terminator is the final content, the same copy reads one byte beyond the input buffer. This issue is fixed in versions 2.9.15 and 3.0.17.

CVE-2026-120640.description:
CGI versions before 5.00 for Perl allow the POSTDATA, PUTDATA, PATCHDATA and XForms:Model parameters to be set from the query string or form fields.

CGI stores a non-form request body under POSTDATA, PUTDATA or PATCHDATA, and an XForms body under XForms:Model, but also accepts these names from the query string, a form field or a multipart part, so an application cannot tell a client-sent value from the real body.

A cross-site HTML form can post POSTDATA={"admin":true} to an endpoint that reads JSON from param('POSTDATA'), a request forgery that needs no CORS preflight.

CVE-2026-122093.title: Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones
CVE-2026-122093.description:
Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones.

The generator keeps its state in a single number. Each call multiplies the state by a factor derived from it, and the returned digits encode that factor, so three consecutive outputs determine the state however the generator was seeded. Outputs are also biased: the first digit after the decimal point is never zero, so rand(256) never returns 1 to 24.

An attacker who sees three consecutive outputs can predict the tokens, passwords or key bytes that the same object later issues to other users.

High-speed devices with out of spec 1024 byte bulk endpoints exist and
are allowed by USB core, but xhci-hcd always sets packet size to 512.
The exact nature of these devices isn't documented, commit fb5ee84ea72c
("USB: Accept bulk endpoints with 1024-byte maxpacket") only states
that they "don't work with xHCI host controllers", whatever it means.

But somebody (or a malicious device) can try, and then the driver will
allocate a 512 byte bounce buffer for this endpoint and may write up to
1024 bytes into it if particular scatter-gather URBs are used, because
xhci_align_td() obtains packet size from the descriptor. Fix this.

As a side effect, TRBs will be aligned to the packet size chosen by the
driver on all endpoints of all speeds. Alignment serves the xHC, not
device, so this is fine. Only out of spec devices are affected anyway.

CVE-2026-99397.title: xfs: always report inode repair setup failures
CVE-2026-99397.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: always report inode repair setup failures

LOLLM noticed that xchk_setup_inode silently discards errors being
returned by xrep_setup_inode. Fix that, and fix the stub macro so that
it actually "returns" a value.
